extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers / writers interested in manners, rhetoric, character, and translation (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing moral/rhetorical essays, letters, and translations: how to portray domestic character and manners, praise without flattery, manage debate rhetorically, and translate faithfully while keeping readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: good Breeding towards a loving and a tender Wife
rubrics_metrics.description: Could you but once convince them, that to be civil at least is not beneath the Character of a Gentleman, nor even tender Affection towards one who would make it reciprocal, betrays any Softness or Effeminacy that the most masculine Disposition need be ashamed of; ... That he thought it incumbent upon him to make the Inclinations of a Woman of Merit go along with her Duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate voluntary civility and benevolence in husbands as a species of greatness of soul; portray such behaviour as reasonable, beautiful, and beneficial to marriage, family happiness, and the wisdom of progeny. Use persuasion to show that civility is compatible with manliness and improves domestic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire to appear free and at Liberty (affected Moroseness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one Cause ... which takes place among the more unthinking Men: and that is the Desire to appear to their Friends free and at Liberty, and without those Trammels they have so much ridiculed. To avoid this they fly into the other Extream, and grow Tyrants that they may seem Masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting characters, show how a motive to appear 'free' can lead to affectation—rigid control of expression, avoidance of kindness (seen as fawning), and a general austerity. Highlight the psychological root (fear of seeming submissive) and the predictable consequences (indifference → contempt → alienation).

rubrics_metrics.name: returning Evil for Good / deceiving a Woman with Appearances of Affection
rubrics_metrics.description: And can there be any thing more base ... than returning Evil for Good in so open a Manner, as that of treating an helpless Creature with Unkindness, who has had so good an Opinion of him ... Must not that Man be abandoned ... who can deceive a Woman with Appearances of Affection and Kindness, for no other End but to torment her with more Ease and Authority?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing moral criticism or characters, mark such conduct as deeply dishonourable. Use explicit moral language and consequences to condemn manipulation that feigns tenderness to control or torment another.

rubrics_metrics.name: seeming Indifference will by Degrees grow into real Contempt (consequences of affectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: his seeming Indifference will by Degrees grow into real Contempt, and if it doth not wholly alienate the Affections of his Wife for ever, make both him and her more miserable than if it really did so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ gradual escalation in narrative: small affectations and feigned indifference should plausibly accumulate into genuine emotional distance—use this as a device to show moral/self-inflicted decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: relieving abstract thought by relating a Tradition/Parable (Moses story)
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall relieve my Reader from this abstracted Thought, by relating here a Jewish Tradition concerning Moses ... which seems to be a kind of Parable, illustrating what I have last mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To explain abstract or theological arguments, use a concise parable or illustrative anecdote. Structure the story so it concretely indexes the abstract claim (e.g., hidden links in Providence), and allow the tale to reveal the intended moral or perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: the Love of Flattery is pernicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all the Diseases of the Mind, there is not one more epidemical or more pernicious than the Love of Flattery. ... First we flatter ourselves, and then the Flattery of others is sure of Success. It awakens our Self-Love within ... and join the Enemy without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In essays and character studies, treat flattery as a moral/psychological corruptor: show how self-deception opens people to influence, and dramatize how flattery compromises judgment and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: praise well (art of praising justly)
rubrics_metrics.description: But if Flattery be the most sordid Act that can be complied with, the Art of Praising justly is as commendable: For tis laudable to praise well; ... that Man is happy in this Art, who, like a skilful Painter, retains the Features and Complection, but still softens the Picture into the most agreeable Likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish praise from flattery in representation: praise should be discerning, proportionate, and faithful to the subject's features while enhancing their agreeable aspects. Use tasteful, precise commendation rather than excessive or insincere adulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: retain Features but soften the Picture (translator/artist guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: like a skilful Painter, retains the Features and Complection, but still softens the Picture into the most agreeable Likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether describing a person, translating a text, or adapting a work, preserve core identity/details (features) but smooth or modestly idealize to produce an agreeable, readable representation—avoid caricature or slavish copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: value of sincere and extorted praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Such was that which Germanicus enjoyed, when, the Night before a Battle, desirous of some sincere Mark of the Esteem of his Legions for him, he is described ... wrapt up in the Fruition of his Glory, whilst with an undesigned Sincerity they praised his noble and majestick Mien ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray sincere, especially unexpected praise (even from enemies) as more valuable and motivating than polite flattery. Use scenes of unforced commendation to reveal character nobility and spur further deeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: be a good Original rather than a miserable Copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tis the Desire of some Quality we are not possessed of, or Inclination to be something we are not, which are the Causes of our giving ourselves up to that Man, who bestows upon us the Characters and Qualities of others; ... Instead of going out of our own complectional Nature into that of others, twere a better and more laudable Industry to improve our own, and instead of a miserable Copy become a good Original;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative practice and character advice, favor cultivation of one's own strengths and voice over imitation. Show characters who strive to improve their native temper and talents rather than adopt alien personas.

rubrics_metrics.name: praise proportion and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: There can hardly, I believe, be imagin'd a more desirable Pleasure, than that of Praise unmix'd with any Possibility of Flattery. ... but if too strongly admitted into a Brain of a less vigorous and happy Texture, twill, like too strong an Odour, overcome the Senses, and prove pernicious ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing praise or critical commentary, calibrate intensity to the audience and subject. Overly extravagant praise can intoxicate or corrupt; measured commendation is healthier and more sustaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: faithful translation: keep as near the Meaning of the Greek as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: In the following Translation, I have kept as near the Meaning of the Greek as I could, and have only added a few Words to make the Sentences in English fit together a little better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating literary material, prioritize fidelity to the original meaning; permit only minimal, necessary additions for natural syntax and readability in the target language. Use small adjustments rather than freer paraphrase when the aim is close rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socratick (catechetical) Method of Arguing
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates introduced a catechetical Method of Arguing. He would ask his Adversary Question upon Question, till he had convinced him out of his own Mouth that his Opinions were wrong. This Way of Debating drives an Enemy up into a Corner, seizes all the Passes through which he can make an Escape, and forces him to surrender at Discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For persuasive writing or dialectical passages, employ the Socratic method: ask a sequence of probing questions that expose contradictions and lead the interlocutor (and reader) to the intended conclusion by their own admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelick method: use of syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle changed this Method of Attack, and invented a great Variety of little Weapons, call'd Syllogisms. ... In the Aristotelick you are still denying and contradicting some Part or other of what he says. Socrates conquers you by Stratagem, Aristotle by Force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing argumentative prose, use formal logical steps—syllogisms and precise objections—to refute specific premises. This method suits analytical critique and systematic polemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentum Basilinum / Club-Law (knock down the opponent)
rubrics_metrics.description: When they were not able to confute their Antagonist, they knock'd him down. It was their Method in these polemical Debates, first to discharge their Syllogisms, and afterwards to betake themselves to their Clubs, till such Time as they had one Way or other confounded their Gainsayers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rhetorical datum: illustrate (and condemn) the move from reasoned argument to brute force. Use this contrast to critique sophistry or show how debates can degrade into coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: arguing by poll and by wagers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a way of managing an Argument not much unlike the former, which is made use of by States and Communities, when they draw up a hundred thousand Disputants on each Side, and convince one another by Dint of Sword. ... There is a way of Reasoning which may be called arguing by Poll; and another in which Wagers are made use of as Arguments ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and depict non-rational modes of 'argument'—majority force (arguing by poll) and gambling/wagers—as persuasive tactics that substitute power, consensus, or risk for reason. Use such modes to expose weaknesses in public reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: arguing by Torture (coerced conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most notable way of managing a Controversy, is that which we may call Arguing by Torture. ... The Rack is also a kind of Syllogism which has been used with good Effect, and has made Multitudes of Converts. ... the Application of Whips, Racks, Gibbets, Gallies, Dungeons, Fire and Faggot, in a Dispute, may be look'd upon as Popish Refinements upon the old Heathen Logick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat coercion as an illegitimate rhetorical device; when describing historical or moral arguments, condemn forced conversions and use them to illustrate moral failure or intellectual bankruptcy.

rubrics_metrics.name: arguing by bribery (ready money)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another way of Reasoning which seldom fails, tho it be of a quite different Nature to that I have last mentioned. I mean, convincing a Man by ready Money, or as it is ordinarily called, bribing a Man to an Opinion. ... Gold is a wonderful Clearer of the Understanding;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose corruption where monetary inducement displaces reason. In persuasive writing or satire, show how wealth can 'clear' objections and win assent—use it to moralize or mock.

rubrics_metrics.name: theatrical/audience conduct should not distract or show off
rubrics_metrics.description: This was a very lusty Fellow, but withal a sort of Beau ... he affected to survey the whole House, bow'd and smil'd at random, and then shew'd his Teeth ... If there were no Injunctions to the contrary, yet this Practice must be confess'd to diminish the Pleasure of the Audience, and for that Reason presumptuous and unwarrantable: But since her Majesty's late Command has made it criminal, you have Authority to take Notice of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting scenes of public performance, mark ostentatious, attention-seeking behaviour as disruptive and presumptuous; use stage directions or narrative condemnation to preserve collective aesthetic experience. Note that authorities or custom may proscribe such behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: church behaviour: repetition of prayers after the minister is offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Disturbance some People give to others at Church, by their Repetition of the Prayers after the Minister ... in a particular Manner the Priests Office: This I have known done in so audible a manner, that sometimes their Voices have been as loud as his. ... This irreligious Inadvertency is a Thing extremely offensive: But I do not recommend it as a Thing I give you Liberty to ridicule, but hope it may be amended by the bare Mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a social-observation rubric: in depictions of piety or communal worship, treat excessive personal performance (e.g., loudly repeating the minister) as inconsiderate and disruptive. Use mild public censure as a corrective rather than ridicule.
